children: Educators emphasise human judgement, responsible AI use and industry exposure as design careers evolve

Indian design institutions are rethinking how they prepare students for careers as artificial intelligence (AI) transforms creative workflows and industry requirements. Educators at the BW Future of Design Summit & Awards 2026, held on 18 September at Novotel Mumbai International Airport, highlighted the need to move beyond placement-focused training towards lifelong learning, human judgement and practical industry exposure.
The discussion, titled ‘Rethinking Design Education’, examined how institutions can integrate AI without compromising creativity, critical thinking and the ability to solve real-world problems.
“Rather than creating an impact and making them ready for their first job, how do we make them ready for an entire career?” said Abir Aich, Executive Vice President, Technical M&E, Aptech Ltd.

Aich said institutions must focus on capabilities that remain relevant throughout a career rather than preparing students solely for their first placement. He called for a shift from industry readiness towards preparing students for future changes.

As AI tools accelerate design production, educators are placing greater emphasis on the creative process and the human judgement required to evaluate outcomes. Aich said AI could generate hundreds of design options, but selecting solutions relevant to a particular problem remains a human responsibility. He argued that AI should be embedded throughout design workflows rather than introduced as a standalone module.

Prof. Shalini Gupta, Dean, School of Complete Professionals, Life Design Studio, AI Studio, Pearl Academy, said institutions must prepare students for an industry that could change substantially during a four-year degree.

“What I can promise you is that I will make you life ready. I will make you a lifelong learner. I will make you resilient,” Gupta said. She said Pearl Academy has adopted an AI-first approach while retaining human judgement and agency. Students are required to document their AI prompts and record how the technology contributes to their work. “We let AI do what AI does best, which is speed and scale. We don't actually depend on it for judgment,” she said.

Design educators also emphasised empathy, behavioural understanding and field research as essential capabilities that cannot be replaced by automated tools. Dr. Arundhati Guha Thakurta, Associate Dean, SVKM’s NMIMS School of Design, said students must understand the people and circumstances behind design problems rather than focus exclusively on technological outputs. Her institution encourages students to undertake foundational exercises using pen and paper while teaching responsible AI use.

It also requires students to complete a month-long internship with a non-governmental organisation (NGO) to develop empathy through direct engagement. “I'm not saying that AI is the problem. It is a reality and we have to deal with it” Thakurta said. She added that AI could support preliminary research, but observing people and understanding their needs required direct human involvement.

Prof. Dr. Milind M Dhobley, Director, School of Design, Dr. D Y Patil Vidyapeeth, Pune, said institutions must connect academic learning with practical industry requirements while encouraging original thinking. His school brings industry professionals onto campus to involve students in live projects from their second year.
“We have brought the industry to our campus. Students are directly engaging in industry projects from the second year onwards,” Dhobley said.

Gupta also highlighted entrepreneurship as a response to employment challenges, citing Pearl Academy's incubation programme, which provides students and faculty with opportunities to pitch ideas, secure grants and receive mentorship. The panel also emphasised developing design solutions suited to India's cultural diversity and local requirements rather than simply replicating international approaches.
